title: Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization
claim: Prior generative samplers trade geometric accuracy for memorization of training points; learning the projection recovers the manifold without memorizing.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, arrow over diffusion panels, gray projection lines in last
description: Three square scatter plots side by side, all showing a unit circle in 2D with 40 red triangles as training points. A long black arrow above the first two panels reads 'Reverse diffusion ODE: time decreases'. Panel 1 (t=10^-3) shows blue generated samples forming a noisy, fuzzy ring with clumps around the red triangles. Panel 2 (t=10^-6) shows a sharper ring but the blue samples cluster tightly on the red triangles, with gaps between them, which indicates memorization. Panel 3, titled 'Projection model', shows a clean, continuous, uniformly covered blue circle. Thin gray dashed lines run from gray noised points scattered around the circle to their projections on it. The eye goes first to the clean circle on the right, then compares it with the clumpy diffusion rings.
caption: Denoising diffusion versus projection learning for the uniform measure on the unit circle in $\mathbb R^2$, trained on $40$ points (red triangles) with $1000$ generated samples (blue). Left: Reverse-ODE diffusion samples at $t=10^{-3},10^{-6}$; smaller time improves geometry but increases memorization near training points. Right: Learned projection of $1000$ noised samples ($\delta=0.7$, gray) identifies the circle precisely with negligible memorization.
abstract: We introduce a framework for learning distributions supported on manifolds based on estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support. Specifically, we define an objective functional over a class of functions whose minimizer recovers this projection. The proposed framework automatically adapts to the intrinsic dimension and allows for data supported on unions of manifolds with varying dimensions. The resulting objective can be optimized using standard neural network architectures. We present population-level results establishing recovery of the manifold projection and prove finite-sample Wasserstein generalization bounds. Furthermore, we validate the approach empirically across a range of settings. In contrast to widely used generative models such as diffusion models, whose objectives can be minimized by memorizing training samples, our formulation excludes such behavior. We also introduce a direct memorization metric to verify that the learned projection generates new samples rather than reproducing the training set.
